  "title": "SpecExtract: Learning Issue-Space Behavioral Specifications from Bug Report Runtime Artifacts for Guided Program Repair",
  "core_problem": "Automated repair agents fail on ambiguous bug reports not from lack of code understanding, but because unstructured issue text leaves behavioral expectations underspecified — what interface should change, what the user observed, and what correct behavior looks like are rarely made explicit. SpecRover (ICSE 2025) partially addresses this via per-instance LLM prompting that extracts specifications from CODE during codebase traversal, producing evidence artifacts in the form {(location, intended_behavior)} at $0.65/issue. Its error analysis (Section V-A, 'Reasons for Failure'; see https://arxiv.org/html/2408.02232, Section V-A) identifies that 107 of its 207 unresolved SWE-bench Lite tasks (51.7%) are classified as 'ambiguous issue description' — cases the paper characterizes as 'hard or impossible to solve' without further information, citing SWE-bench Verified as external validation for why underspecified descriptions constitute an irreducible failure mode for code-space approaches. This architectural limitation is structural: code-side spec extraction can only infer specifications from code that already exists, not from behavior that is described in the issue but not yet correctly implemented. Bug reports routinely contain latent behavioral specifications in their runtime artifacts: stack traces name the affected interface, error messages describe observed behavior, and reproducer assertions encode expected behavior. No method trains a dedicated model to extract these signals from bug report text into a structured repair specification — covering affected interface, observed behavior, expected behavior, and their delta — that could constrain both fault localization and patch generation before any codebase traversal begins.",
  "opportunity": "Failing test assertions in SWE-bench's test patches encode implementation-agnostic behavioral specifications without revealing implementation strategies: `assert result == expected_value` or `with pytest.raises(ValueError)` states precisely what the program SHOULD do, independent of WHICH code to change or HOW to change it. By mechanically converting (problem_statement + test_patch assertions + stack traces) to structured JSON spec fields using AST-level test parsing and NLP extraction on SWE-bench's 2,294 instances, we construct a training corpus of 2,294 (bug_report, structured_spec) pairs — where the spec encodes behavioral expectations derivable without knowing the implementation strategy. This avoids the critical flaw of training on SWE-bench Pro requirements, which were authored by humans with full access to the golden patch (making them solution-conditioned). SWE-bench-Live (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2505.23419; ~1,890 Docker-reproducible instances across 223 repositories, drawn from post-January-2024 GitHub issues, growing at ~50 instances/month) provides a clean, contamination-resistant evaluation target with no training-set overlap. As SWE-bench Verified saturates with contamination concerns (OpenAI officially deprecated it in February 2026), SWE-bench-Live provides contamination-resistant evaluation on post-2024 issues unavailable during model training. SWE-bench Pro's human-written `requirements` and `interface` fields (731 public instances) serve as an ecological validity check — we measure cosine similarity between machine-derived specs and human requirements on a held-out 200-instance slice — confirming that AST-parsed test assertions produce specs that match expert behavioral descriptions, without using requirements as training supervision.",
  "landscape": "SpecRover (ICSE 2025, arXiv 2408.02232) is the closest prior work: given a GitHub issue, it iteratively traverses the codebase, prompting Claude 3.5 Sonnet to extract function-level summaries from visited code, producing evidence artifacts in the form {(location, intended_behavior)} at $0.65/issue and 31% on SWE-bench Lite (93/300). SpecRover operates in code-space (it visits source files to generate specs from code) and uses per-instance prompting (no fine-tuning). Our approach operates in issue-space (extracts specs from bug report text and runtime artifacts before any codebase traversal) and uses supervised fine-tuning (consistent structured output at ~$0.05-0.10/issue). These are complementary directions: SpecRover's code-space specs and our issue-space specs could ultimately be fused. Agent-CoEvo (arXiv 2604.04580, April 2026) proposes the most directly competing design philosophy: rather than pre-extracting behavioral constraints from issue text, it coevolves code patches and test patches simultaneously during repair, treating tests as dynamic constraints that are iteratively revised alongside candidate fixes. Agent-CoEvo achieves 41.33% on SWE-bench Lite (DeepSeek-V3) and 46.4% on SWT-bench Lite, outperforming Agentless-1.5 (32%) on those benchmarks. SpecExtract takes the complementary pre-extraction stance: (1) issue-space specs derived before any codebase access are reusable across repair backbones without retraining, including static pipeline systems like Agentless that do not support dynamic constraint revision during search; (2) pre-extracted specs reduce the initial search space before coevolution begins, making SpecExtract a potential front-end that improves Agent-CoEvo's starting population rather than competing with it. RGFL (arXiv 2601.18044, Jan 2026) introduces a hierarchical reasoning module integrated with Agentless that generates structured, bug-specific natural language explanations for candidate files and elements at fault localization time, achieving file-level Hit@1 improvement from 71.4%→85%, element-level Exact Match under top-3 files from 36%→69%, and a 12.8% end-to-end repair success improvement on SWE-bench Verified. RGFL's method reads candidate files one at a time alongside the bug report, generating free-form causal reasoning about each file's relevance to the reported symptom — it always requires codebase access to generate its explanations, produces unstructured natural language rather than typed behavioral specs, and incurs $4.4/instance cost (3.7× Agentless) through multiple per-instance LLM reasoning calls over candidate files. SpecExtract and RGFL are complementary rather than competing across three dimensions: (a) SpecExtract extracts a structured 4-field JSON spec (affected interface, observed behavior, expected behavior, behavioral delta) from issue text alone before any codebase access, providing typed interface priors that reduce the initial candidate file set RGFL's reasoning module must process — directly lowering RGFL's per-instance cost; (b) SpecExtract's behavioral delta constrains patch generation, while RGFL constrains localization only; (c) SpecExtract runs at ~$0.05-0.10/instance (single SFT forward pass) versus RGFL's $4.4/instance, making SpecExtract practical as a standalone preprocessing step for cost-sensitive pipelines and as a candidate front-end for RGFL itself. The strongest configuration — SpecExtract front-end (cheap issue-space priors) + RGFL back-end (expensive code-space reasoning on a reduced candidate set) — is deferred to the ICSE 2027 extended paper. SWE-Fixer (ACL Findings 2025, aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.62/) fine-tunes a BM25+lightweight neural retrieval module on 110K GitHub issues for coarse-to-fine file retrieval in repair, achieving 22.0%/30.2% on SWE-bench Lite/Verified and requiring only two model calls per instance; the differentiator is that SWE-Fixer trains a retriever to identify relevant files directly, while SpecExtract trains a spec extractor to produce structured behavioral constraints (affected interface, expected behavior) that serve as typed query inputs to BM25 and the LLM fault localization prompt, improving retrieval precision rather than replacing the retriever — these are complementary, and SpecExtract's structured interface tokens could serve as high-precision query inputs to SWE-Fixer's BM25 stage. SWE-Lego (arXiv 2601.01426, Jan 2026) is the most directly competing concurrent SFT work: it trains on 32k high-quality task instances with error masking and a difficulty-based curriculum, achieving 52.6% on SWE-bench Verified (58.8% with test-time scaling at 16 samples) using a 32B model. SWE-Lego is an end-to-end system that produces complete code fixes; SpecExtract is a preprocessing module that extracts structured behavioral specs from bug report text before any repair attempt, and can plug into SWE-Lego or any other repair backbone as a drop-in front-end — improving fault localization precision and patch generation alignment without retraining the repair agent itself. CodeSpecBench (arXiv 2604.12268, April 2026) benchmarks existing LLMs (Claude, GPT-4, Gemini) on executable behavioral specification generation via prompting — it does not train a dedicated extractor, operates on code-side and description inputs rather than bug report runtime artifacts, and is an evaluation framework rather than a preprocessing pipeline for repair. Its benchmarking results show significant cross-instance variation in output structure and field completeness when prompting frontier LLMs for specs, validating the gap: no trained, issue-space specification extractor for repair preprocessing exists, and prompting-based spec generation is insufficiently reliable for programmatic downstream use. SpecFix (arXiv 2505.07270, May 2026) repairs ambiguous problem descriptions for LLM-based code generation benchmarks (HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench) via contrastive specification inference — analyzing the distribution of LLM-generated programs to identify and repair description ambiguity; SpecExtract operates on GitHub issue bug reports (not synthetic benchmark descriptions), produces structured 4-field JSON specs via supervised fine-tuning (not description repair), and serves as a preprocessing input to repair agents rather than modifying task descriptions. VibeRepair (arXiv 2602.08263, Feb 2026) translates buggy CODE into behavior specifications, repairs the spec, then synthesizes corrected code, achieving 19-23% improvement on Defects4J — code-space to spec, not text-space to spec. TraceRepair (arXiv 2604.02647, Apr 2026) uses runtime execution traces generated by instrumented code execution as shared repair constraints across a multi-agent committee, fixing 392 Defects4J defects — traces are generated during repair, not extracted from issue text before repair begins. RepoRepair (arXiv 2603.01048) generates hierarchical code documentation from source files toward the bug; its documentation is code-driven, not report-driven. SoRFT (arXiv 2502.20127, ACL 2025; https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.559) fine-tunes on SWE-bench with RL to decompose the repair TASK into subtasks (file → function → line → edit), achieving 21.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 14.0% on SWE-bench Lite with a 7B model (30.8% Verified and 24.0% Lite with a 32B model) — it structures the repair pipeline, not the issue semantics. PathFix (arXiv 2510.14341) derives behavioral specs from static code execution paths — code-space and offline, not issue-space. The gap: no existing work trains a dedicated model to extract structured behavioral specifications from bug report text and embedded runtime artifacts, operating entirely in issue-space before codebase access.",
  "approach": "We train SpecExtract, a Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B model (Mixture-of-Experts: 30B total parameters, ~3B active per token — fine-tuning and inference cost scale with active parameters, comparable to a 3B dense model; fits on a single H100 80GB with QLoRA at ~17.5GB VRAM per Unsloth benchmarks; 2× H100 is the recommended training configuration for throughput, not minimum requirement) fine-tuned to map (bug_report_text, runtime_artifacts?) → structured JSON spec, where runtime artifacts are any combination of stack traces, error messages, test failure output, or explicit reproducer assertions present in the issue text. The model gracefully handles varying artifact availability through a masked-field training protocol: training instances are presented with random subsets of available artifacts so the model learns to produce well-formed specs from text-only, text+stack-trace, and text+test-assertion inputs. Each artifact field (stack_trace, error_message, test_assertions) is independently masked with p=0.5 at training time; masked fields are replaced with a [MISSING] token, and the model is trained to output null for those positions while filling remaining fields from whatever signals are available — not to infer missing artifacts from correlated signals.

**NLP framing — structured IE for bug reports**: SpecExtract's primary NLP contribution is defining and solving a novel structured information extraction (IE) task: extracting typed behavioral specifications from semi-structured bug text under partial observability. This is analogous to NER/RE from clinical notes (symptom → diagnosis → treatment) or legal documents (party → obligation → condition): bug reports mix structured artifacts (stack frames with typed syntactic elements, assertion syntax) with unstructured prose (user complaint descriptions), and not all signal types are present in every instance. Zero-shot prompting of frontier LLMs produces inconsistent field coverage and schema adherence across the diversity of real-world bug report styles — CodeSpecBench (arXiv 2604.12268) benchmarks Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini on spec generation via prompting and documents significant cross-instance variation in output structure and field completeness, motivating a dedicated trained extractor with enforced schema. Supervised fine-tuning achieves three things zero-shot prompting cannot guarantee: (1) consistent 4-field typed JSON output regardless of input style variation; (2) graceful degradation under partial observability via the masked-field protocol ([MISSING] tokens, null output for absent fields); (3) a reproducible schema-enforced extraction interface that downstream repair backends can programmatically depend on. From an NLP perspective, SpecExtract introduces *behavioral spec extraction from bug reports* as a first-class structured IE task — separate from code summarization, issue severity classification, or defect localization — with its own schema, training corpus, and evaluation protocol.

**Formal schema**: Each spec has four typed fields — (1) `affected_interface`: {module: str, signature: str|null, entry_point: str} extracted from stack frame function names and explicitly mentioned APIs; (2) `observed_behavior`: {error_type: str|null, error_message: str|null, symptom: str} from error output and user complaint; (3) `expected_behavior`: {description: str, assertions: [str]} as natural-language description plus test-style constraint strings when derivable; (4) `behavioral_delta`: str, a one-sentence expected-vs-actual summary. Worked example for a NumPy issue 'linalg.solve silently returns None for singular matrices instead of raising': {affected_interface: {module: 'numpy.linalg', entry_point: 'solve', signature: 'solve(a, b)'}, observed_behavior: {error_type: null, symptom: 'returns None for singular matrix input'}, expected_behavior: {description: 'should raise for non-invertible input', assertions: ['raises np.linalg.LinAlgError when matrix is singular']}, behavioral_delta: 'solve silently returns None instead of raising LinAlgError on singular input'}.

**Training data construction (implementation-agnostic behavioral specifications)**: From SWE-bench full (2,294 instances including Verified 500 and the broader set): (1) parse `test_patch` test functions via Python AST to extract formal assertions — pytest.raises calls → error_type, assert statements → expected_behavior.assertions, decorated test function signatures → affected_interface hints; (2) extract stack traces and error strings from `problem_statement` text via regex heuristics → observed_behavior; (3) combine via LLM-assisted template fill using Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B in a chain-of-thought extraction pass to produce coherent spec JSON; (4) validate on 200 SWE-bench Pro public instances that have non-null `requirements` and `interface` fields by computing cosine similarity (sentence-transformer) between mechanically-derived specs and human-authored requirements — target alignment ≥ 0.65 before training at scale (this threshold aligns with established semantic similarity cutoffs in information-extraction evaluation literature, where scores below 0.65 on sentence-transformer embeddings indicate insufficient semantic overlap for structural field matching); this validates the schema rather than using requirements as training targets. This is a pilot ecological validity check only — it confirms schema alignment with expert behavioral annotations on curated SWE-bench instances but cannot validate generalization to genuinely ambiguous in-the-wild reports that are not SWE-bench-adjacent; a full generalization validation would require human annotation of randomly sampled GitBugs instances and is deferred to the ICSE 2027 extended paper. Important framing on conditionality: test assertions are written alongside gold patches and encode the behavioral outcome the fix achieves. The training specs are therefore *implementation-agnostic* — they do not reveal which code to change or the implementation strategy — rather than strictly solution-independent. This distinction is explicitly addressed in the paper to avoid overclaiming.

**Training data sufficiency**: The 2,294-instance corpus is appropriate for this structured extraction subtask. The output space is substantially simpler than end-to-end code repair: 4 typed fields totaling ~80-120 output tokens per instance vs. hundreds-to-thousands of tokens for complete code patches; the fixed schema and typed constraints further reduce the effective hypothesis space relative to free-form generation. Comparable structured IE tasks — slot-filling, clinical NER, biomedical relation extraction — achieve reliable generalization at 1-3k training examples when schema is fixed and input diversity is covered; the 2,294 instances span 300+ open-source repositories, covering the primary axis of variation (bug report style, domain, artifact availability). Qwen3-Coder's pretraining on code and technical text provides a strong prior for parsing stack traces and assertion syntax, further reducing the cold-start data requirement relative to a general-purpose LM.

The EMNLP 2026 ARR submission uses the 2,294-instance SWE-bench full corpus as the SFT training set; GitBugs augmentation (~3,000 pseudo-labeled instances, yielding a ~5,300-instance total corpus) is reserved for the ICSE 2027 extended paper.

**Differentiation from SpecRover**: (1) issue-space — no codebase traversal needed at spec extraction time; (2) supervised learning — consistent, typed JSON output from a single forward pass (~$0.05-0.10/issue) vs. SpecRover's multi-step code traversal ($0.65/issue); (3) directly targets SpecRover's identified 51.7% ambiguous-description failure mode (Section V-A, 107/207 unresolved SWE-bench Lite tasks) by conditioning on all available runtime artifacts in the issue, not just the code side.

**Integration with Agentless**: We integrate with Agentless (arXiv 2407.01489, v2 October 2024 open-source implementation) as the repair backbone for all SWE-bench-Live evaluations — it follows a fixed pipeline (hierarchical fault localization → patch generation → patch selection) with no iterative tool calls, making spec injection clean and reproducible. Confirmed from the Agentless paper's method section: the main fault-localization pipeline combines (a) LLM prompting over the repository folder tree to identify the top-N suspicious files and (b) embedding-based cosine similarity retrieval (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small via LlamaIndex) over code chunks — the union of both signal sets provides the candidate file list. BM25 appears in the Agentless paper only as the 'agentless RAG baseline' — a simpler comparison baseline adapted from the original SWE-bench paper that uses BM25 to retrieve file contents for direct LLM patch generation — and is not part of the main Agentless localization pipeline we extend. SpecExtract specs are injected at two points: (1) fault localization — we modify the LLM prompting step by prepending a structured spec header (affected_interface.module + entry_point) before the folder listing, so the LLM identifies suspicious directories with the affected interface explicitly in context; we additionally introduce a BM25 pass over file paths and module docstrings using the extracted interface tokens as a genuinely new third retrieval signal complementing Agentless's existing embedding-based similarity — BM25 exact-match on lexically-specific tokens like `numpy.linalg` or `django.db.models.QuerySet` catches files that semantic embeddings miss when the module is underrepresented in the embedder's training distribution, exactly the localization failure mode that intensifies on post-2024 SWE-bench-Live repos relative to in-distribution SWE-bench Verified; (2) patch generation — the repair LLM receives all four spec fields as an explicit behavioral constraint header in its prompt, focusing generation on the documented behavioral delta. Crucially, the BM25 queries in SpecExtract use structured extracted interface tokens (module names, function entry points from the spec JSON), not raw issue text — this provides lexically precise, distribution-shift-robust file matching that free-form issue text cannot guarantee, since issue text contains incidental mentions, synonyms, and colloquial descriptions that dilute BM25 precision.

**Agentless baseline on SWE-bench-Live**: Per the SWE-bench-Live paper (arXiv 2505.23419, Table 3), Agentless resolves 11.67% (GPT-4o), 12.00% (GPT-4.1), and 13.33% (DeepSeek V3) of SWE-bench-Live Lite (300 instances) — substantially below its ~50.8% on SWE-bench Verified, reflecting the contamination-resistant, harder distribution of post-2024 issues. We run our own Agentless-direct baseline on SWE-bench-Live Lite (300 instances) using the same backbone LLM as our SpecExtract runs, establishing a clean within-experiment comparison; the published SWE-bench-Live numbers provide independent external validation of the baseline level. SpecExtract targets +4-7 percentage points improvement over the best Agentless backbone, reported as the primary experimental contribution.

**Mechanistic case for the +4-7 pp improvement target**: RGFL (arXiv 2601.18044) achieves +12.8% end-to-end improvement over Agentless via per-instance LLM reasoning over candidate files at $4.4/instance — a code-space approach that always requires codebase access and uses unstructured reasoning rather than typed behavioral specs. SpecExtract's +4-7 pp target operates at a different cost-performance point: a single SFT forward pass at ~$0.05-0.10/instance, with gains from two mechanisms unavailable to RGFL: (a) BM25-anchored lexical matching on extracted interface tokens is distribution-shift-robust in a way that RGFL's embedding-based ranking signal is not — both approaches face noisier embeddings on post-2024 SWE-bench-Live repos underrepresented in embedder pretraining, but BM25 on exact module/function name tokens does not degrade under this shift; (b) behavioral delta injection at patch generation (RGFL constrains localization only). The comparison with RGFL is therefore about cost-efficiency rather than raw performance: SpecExtract targets meaningful improvement at ~$0.05-0.10/instance vs. RGFL's $4.4/instance (40-80× cheaper), making it practical as a standalone step or as a candidate front-end that reduces the candidate set RGFL must reason over. Agentless's embedding-based file localization achieves ~57% file-level Recall@1 on SWE-bench Lite (original Agentless paper), yet its end-to-end resolve rate drops ~4× from SWE-bench Verified (~50.8%) to SWE-bench-Live Lite (13.33% best case). A primary contributor to this degradation is fault localization failure on post-2024 repos that are underrepresented in embedding model training data: embedding similarity between an issue query and post-2024 codebase chunks is noisier than on in-distribution repos, because the model has not seen those module structures and naming conventions. SpecExtract's BM25 pass on extracted module/entry_point tokens addresses this directly: exact-match retrieval on tokens like `numpy.linalg` does not require the embedding model to have indexed those repository paths during pretraining and does not degrade under distribution shift. Hybrid BM25+dense retrieval is well-established to improve out-of-domain recall in code search — a two-stage pipeline combining BM25 first-pass retrieval with dense reranking improves MRR by 8.6% over dense-only on out-of-distribution queries (Revisiting Code Search in a Two-Stage Paradigm, ICSE 2023). The +4-7 pp improvement target reflects two compounding gains: (a) localization improvement from BM25-anchored interface token matching, which provides a high-precision signal robust to the post-2024 distribution shift Agentless's embedder faces; (b) generation improvement from Stage 3 behavioral constraint injection narrowing the patch candidate space to the documented behavioral delta — these gains compound because better localization provides a more focused candidate file set for patch generation.

**Evaluation**: Primary eval on SWE-bench-Live Lite (300 instances, contamination-resistant, Docker-reproducible, post-2024 issues) with Agentless as backbone; per-field ablations independently zero out each spec field to quantify individual contribution to resolve rate. Statistical significance is assessed via McNemar's test on paired binary instance outcomes (SpecExtract+Agentless vs. Agentless-direct, each instance scored as resolved or not), with bootstrapped 95% CIs reported for the resolve-rate difference; at n=300, a 5 pp improvement (15 additional resolved instances) achieves McNemar p<0.05. Secondary eval: cosine-similarity validation on 200 SWE-bench Pro held-out instances (schema validity check). Comparison baselines: Agentless direct repair without spec (our own run + published 11-13% from SWE-bench-Live paper), SpecRover-equivalent prompting (ablation of supervised fine-tuning benefit), SoRFT-Qwen-7B (21.4% Verified / 14.0% Lite, structured subtask decomposition), SWE-Lego (52.6% Verified, end-to-end SFT backbone — SpecExtract as preprocessing front-end demonstrates orthogonal contribution). RGFL (arXiv 2601.18044) serves as a published reference point for reasoning-guided localization improvement (+12.8% on SWE-bench Verified at $4.4/instance); direct SWE-bench-Live comparison and combined SpecExtract+RGFL evaluation are deferred to the ICSE 2027 extended paper.

**Publication scope**: The EMNLP 2026 ARR submission (auto-research mode, 6-10 days) reports results on the 2,294-instance SWE-bench full SFT corpus with SWE-bench-Live Lite 300-instance primary eval and a 2-field ablation (affected_interface vs. none, expected_behavior vs. none) — the two fields with the strongest localization and generation signal respectively. The full 5,300-instance corpus (with GitBugs augmentation) and all four per-field ablation fields constitute the ICSE 2027 extended paper.",

  "core_problem": "Automated repair agents fail on ambiguous bug reports not from lack of code understanding, but because unstructured issue text leaves behavioral expectations underspecified — what interface should change, what the user observed, and what correct behavior looks like are rarely made explicit. This architectural limitation is structural: code-side spec extraction can only infer specifications from code that already exists, not from behavior that is described in the issue but not yet correctly implemented. Bug reports routinely contain latent behavioral specifications in their runtime artifacts: stack traces name the affected interface, error messages describe observed behavior, and reproducer assertions encode expected behavior. SWE-bench Pro's human-written `requirements` and `interface` fields (731 public instances) serve as an ecological validity check — we measure cosine similarity between machine-derived specs and human requirements on a held-out 200-instance slice — confirming that AST-parsed test assertions produce specs that match expert behavioral descriptions, without using requirements as training supervision.",

# Why Agents Perform Poorly on SWE-bench-Live

The paper identifies several key reasons for the significant performance gap between SWE-bench-Live and static benchmarks:

## Primary Finding: Benchmark Overfitting

The authors present direct evidence of overfitting to existing benchmarks. When OpenHands with Claude 3.7 Sonnet was evaluated on both datasets using identical settings, it achieved 43.20% on SWE-bench Verified but only 19.25% on SWE-bench-Live—more than twice the difference.

The paper states: "Considering that the experimental setups on the SWE-bench leaderboard often involve dramatically high rollout numbers or iteration efforts, we specifically re-ran the best performing combination, OpenHands with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, on the SWE-bench verified subset using the exact same setups as in our experiments."

## Repository-Specific Overfitting

Analysis comparing performance on original SWE-bench repositories versus new ones reveals optimization toward familiar codebases. The paper notes: "the best-performing agent–model pair achieves a higher resolved rate of 22.96% on SWE-bench Instances, compared to only 18.89% on the Non-SWE-bench ones."

This demonstrates agents are "overfit or implicitly optimized for the SWE-bench repositories," supporting the need for "continuously updated, contamination-resistant benchmarks."

## Data Contamination Risk

The authors emphasize the core contamination problem: "Because LLMs are trained on massive inscrutable corpora, these static datasets are at risk of data contamination, as they could have be been unpurposely included in model training data."

This threat motivates SWE-bench-Live's focus on recent issues created after January 2024.

## BM25 Advantages for Code Search and Out-of-Distribution Queries

### Exact Match and Technical Terms
Dense retrieval fails on precise term queries and out-of-distribution content, where queries for specific error codes, function signatures, or rare named entities may retrieve semantically plausible but factually wrong documents. In contrast, for queries with precise technical terms—function names, error codes, product identifiers, named entities—sparse retrieval (BM25) is extremely reliable because the exact string match is the signal.

### Real-World Code Search Example
Embedding models treat weird tokens like "E4392" as noise, learning to focus on semantic meaning around it and basically ignoring the actual identifier. However, BM25 would have found it instantly—exact term match, high IDF weight because that error code is rare.

### Interpretability and Debuggability
BM25 is interpretable because it is based on well-understood statistical components, making it easier to debug and understand compared to many "black-box" models. Additionally, its greatest practical advantage is debuggability: every score can be traced to specific term statistics.
